'''Thomas J. Jentsch''' (born April 24, 1953) is a German molecular physiologist and expert in ion‑transport biology whose work has helped shape the understanding of chloride channel families and their role in human physiology and disease.<ref>{{cite web |title=Twenty-five years ago Professor Thomas Jentsch opened up a new field of research |url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2015-09-twenty-five-years-professor-thomas-jentsch.html |website=Medical Xpress}}</ref> He leads the Section for Physiology and Pathology of Ion Transport at the [[Leibniz-Forschungsinstitut für Molekulare Pharmakologie]] (FMP) in Berlin and has also been affiliated (until 2023) with the [[Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association|Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine]]. His research includes the cloning, structural and functional characterisation of the CLC (chloride channel/Cl⁻/H⁺‑exchanger) gene family, the discovery of their roles in human disorders (such as myotonia, osteopetrosis, kidney disease), and the more recent identification of volume‑regulated anion channels (VRAC) and acid‑activated anion channels (ASOR). His lab has also identified the four neuronal members of the KCNQ (Kv7) family of potassium channels and discovered their role in epilepsy and deafness, and studied the roles of all KCC potassium-chloride cotransporters using genetic mouse models. <ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Jentsch |first1=Thomas J. |title=Discovery of CLC transport proteins: cloning, structure, function and pathophysiology |journal=The Journal of Physiology |date=15 September 2015 |volume=593 |issue=18 |pages=4091–4109 |doi=10.1113/JP270043 |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4594286/ |issn=1469-7793|pmc=4594286 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Thomas J. Jentsch |url=https://leibniz-fmp.de/research/research-section/molecular-physiology-cell-biology/thomas-j-jentsch |website=leibniz-fmp.de |language=en |date=18 September 2025}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Thomas J. Jentsch studied both medicine and physics at the [[Freie Universität Berlin]].<ref name=":0" /> He obtained doctoral degrees in both the Dr. rer. nat. (physics) and the Dr. med. (medicine) at the same institution.<ref name=":1" /> Following his doctoral work, Jentsch carried out post‑doctoral research in transport physiology in Berlin and at the [[Whitehead Institute]]/ MIT in the United States, working with [[Harvey Lodish]].<ref name=":0" />

==Research and career==
In 1988 Jentsch was a founding member of the [[Center for Molecular Neurobiology Hamburg]] (ZMNH).<ref name=":0" /> In 2006 he moved his laboratory to Berlin, joining the [[Leibniz-Forschungsinstitut für Molekulare Pharmakologie]] (FMP)  and the [[Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association]] (MDC)'''.'''<ref name=":0" /> His laboratory's research spans from molecular and structural biology of ion channels to their integration in cell biology, physiology and disease.<ref name=":1" /> Jentsch's group made seminal contributions to the identification and functional analysis of the CLC family of chloride channels and Cl⁻/H⁺ exchangers in mammals.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=CLC Cl - channels and transporters |url=https://www.mdc-berlin.de/content/clc-cl-channels-and-transporters |access-date=2025-11-12 |website=www.mdc-berlin.de |language=en}}</ref> They also more recently found that the volume‑regulated anion channel (VRAC) is composed of LRRC8 heteromers and molecularly identified the acid‑activated anion channel (ASOR/TMEM206), another key Cl⁻ channel with physiological relevance.<ref name=":0" />

== Major discoveries and contributions ==
One of Jentsch's main achievements is the cloning and characterisation of the CLC gene family, which comprises nine members in humans and reveals a dramatic diversity of function, from plasma‑membrane chloride channels regulating membrane excitability to intracellular Cl⁻/H⁺ exchangers modulating endolysosomal acidification.<ref name=":2" /> His 2015 review “Discovery of CLC transport proteins: cloning, structure, function and pathophysiology” outlines the path from ClC‑0 to a broad understanding of ion transport and disease.<ref name=":1" /> His work demonstrated that mutations in CLC genes underlie a range of human genetic diseases - for example, myotonia congenita (CLCN1), Bartter syndrome (ClC‑K/barttin), osteopetrosis (ClC‑7/Ostm1) - thereby linking basic channel biology to translational and clinical relevance.<ref name=":1" /> Through his structural‑functional studies, Jentsch helped reveal how channel architecture controls transport properties, and how intracellular chloride transporters contribute to vesicular and lysosomal function, neuronal health, bone resorption, and kidney physiology.<ref name="Jentsch 2002 503–568">{{Cite journal |last=Jentsch |first=Thomas J. |last2=Stein |first2=Valentin |last3=Weinreich |first3=Frank |last4=Zdebik |first4=Anselm A. |date=2002 |title=Molecular Structure and Physiological Function of Chloride Channels |url=https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00029.2001 |journal=Physiological Reviews |volume=82 |issue=2 |pages=503–568 |doi=10.1152/physrev.00029.2001 |issn=0031-9333|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Awards and Honours==
Thomas J. Jentsch has received numerous awards over his career, reflecting contributions to ion-channel biology. In 1995, he was awarded the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize]] by the [[German Research Foundation]] (DFG) for his work on chloride channels.<ref name=":0" /> He has been awarded [[European Research Council]] (ERC) Advanced Grants, first in 2011 and again in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NeuroCure researchers awarded prestigious EU grant - NeuroCure {{!}} Cluster of Excellence |url=https://neurocure.de/118/neurocure-researchers-awarded-prestigious-eu-grant.html?utm |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=neurocure.de}}</ref> In recognition of his scientific achievements, he was granted an Honorary Doctorate (Dr. h.c.) by the [[University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-14 |title=Honorary doctorate conferred on Thomas J. Jentsch |url=https://www.mdc-berlin.de/news/news/honorary-doctorate-conferred-thomas-j-jentsch |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=www.mdc-berlin.de |language=en}}</ref> He has also received the International Prize for Translational Neuroscience <ref>https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Prize_for_Translational_Neuroscience</ref> <ref> https://gertrud-reemtsma-stiftung.sf.mpg.de/prize/ </ref> (1999), the [[Hansen Family Award]]  (2000), [[Feldberg Foundation]] Prize (2000), the Hodgkin-Huxley-Katz Prize Lecture (2006), Adolf-Fick Prize (2004), Homer W. Smith Award for Nephrology (2004), and the [[Ernst Jung Prize]] for medicine (2001).<ref name=":0" /> In 2018, he was awarded the “Gesellschaft braucht Wissenschaft” (“Society needs Science”) Prize by the Stifterverband, and in 2024 he became an Honorary Member of the German Physiological Society.<ref name=":0" />  In 2000, Jentsch was awarded the [[Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine]] by the Fondation Louis-Jeantet.<ref>{{cite web |title=Prize Winners – Fondation Louis-Jeantet |url=https://www.jeantet.ch/en/prizes-louis-jeantet/prize-winners/
 |website=jeantet.ch}}</ref> He is a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]], the [[Academia Europaea]], the [[Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher Leopoldina]], the [[Academy of Sciences and Humanities in Hamburg]] and the  [[Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mitglied – Berlin-Brandenburgische Akademie der Wissenschaften |url=https://www.bbaw.de/die-akademie/bbaw-mitglieder/mitglied-thomas-jentsch?utm |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=www.bbaw.de}}</ref>
